Wideness
WYDE-ness
n. (breadth; the measure of a space across)
From wide, Old English wid, with the suffix -ness. The Hebrew rochab means breadth, from rachab, to be broad.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

In the long measuring of Ezekiel's temple vision, one dimension is given this name: “And between the chambers was the wideness of twenty cubits round about the house on every side” (Ezekiel 41:10). Wideness is simply breadth, and it is worth an entry because of the work the measuring does in these chapters. Ezekiel is shown the house by a man with a line of flax and a measuring reed, and the command given him is explicit: “behold with thine eyes, and hear with thine ears, and set thine heart upon all that I shall shew thee; for to the intent that I might shew them unto thee art thou brought hither: declare all that thou seest to the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 40:4). The purpose of the measurements is then stated: “shew the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities: and let them measure the pattern” (Ezekiel 43:10). The exactness is the message. A people who had defiled a temple are given a house measured to the cubit, with a fixed wideness between the chambers, and told to measure the pattern. Holiness has dimensions, and they are God's to set.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): WIDENESS, breadth; width; great extent between the sides.

WIDENESS, n. Breadth; width; great extent between the sides.

Large extent in all directions.

WIDE, a. Broad; having a great distance or extent between the sides.

Hebrew rochab, breadth, from rachab, to be broad.

Ezekiel 41:10 gives the wideness of twenty cubits between the chambers.

Key Scripture

Eze 41:10 — "And between the chambers was the wideness of twenty cubits round about the house on every side."

Eze 40:4 — "And the man said unto me, Son of man, behold with thine eyes, and hear with thine ears, and set thine heart upon all that I shall shew thee; for to the intent that I might shew them unto thee art thou brought hither: declare all that thou seest to the house of Israel."

Eze 43:10 — "Thou son of man, shew the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities: and let them measure the pattern."

Modern Corruption

Ezekiel's measured temple is pressed into a timetable for a rebuilt sacrificial house, or waved away as meaningless detail, and in both cases the stated purpose of the measuring is lost.

expand to see more

Dispensational premillennialism reads Ezekiel 40 to 48 as the blueprint of a literal millennial temple with restored animal sacrifices. The dictionary rejects dispensationalism as a nineteenth-century novelty absent from every Reformation confession, and rejects this reading in particular because Hebrews forecloses it: there remaineth no more offering for sin, and to reinstitute the shadow would be to deny the finished work. The opposite error treats the chapters as unintelligible and skips them.

Ezekiel himself gives the purpose, and it is neither a construction schedule nor nothing. The house is shewn that Israel may be ashamed of their iniquities and measure the pattern. The exact wideness between the chambers preaches that God, not the worshipper, sets the dimensions of holiness; and the vision ends with the river and the name of the city, The LORD is there. Christ is the temple, His body the house, and His people the measured dwelling of God by the Spirit.
